topic: Spaced retrieval practice: how to keep a newly learned work skill from fading (topic chosen by the knowledge writer because none was supplied; the human must confirm or replace it)
scope_note: Only the core idea: revisit new material in spaced, effortful recall attempts instead of one block. No learning-styles claims, no percentages, no brain-science mechanisms beyond what is stated.

facts.statement: Memory for newly learned material fades over time when it is not used or revisited.
facts.reference_hint: Ebbinghaus, work on memory and forgetting (1885)

facts.statement: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning and slows down as time passes.
facts.reference_hint: Ebbinghaus (1885), the forgetting curve; shape replicated in later work
facts.caveat: The exact rate varies with the material, the person and how well it was learned, so the lesson should describe the shape and give no figures.

facts.statement: The spacing effect: practice spread over several sessions with gaps usually leads to better long-term retention than the same amount of practice in one block.
facts.reference_hint: Cepeda and colleagues, review of spacing studies (2006)
facts.caveat: Best gap length depends on how long the person needs to remember; say 'usually' and give no ideal gap.

facts.statement: Cramming in one block can feel productive and can help for a test soon after, but it tends to fade faster.
facts.caveat: Cramming does work for very short-term needs; the claim is about lasting retention.

facts.statement: Retrieval practice means trying to recall something from memory without looking at it, such as answering a question or doing the task from memory.
Trying to recall material usually strengthens later memory more than simply re-reading or re-watching it.
facts.reference_hint: Roediger and Karpicke (2006), the testing effect
facts.caveat: Effect is strongest when recall is attempted before checking the answer; feedback afterwards helps.

facts.statement: Re-reading or re-watching material can feel familiar and easy, and that feeling of familiarity can be mistaken for knowing it.
facts.caveat: Describes a common pattern, not every learner in every case.

facts.statement: Recall attempts that feel somewhat hard, even when some answers are wrong or missed, tend to help learning more than ones that feel effortless.
facts.caveat: Difficulty must stay manageable; impossible tasks without feedback do not help. Often called 'desirable difficulty'.

facts.statement: A practical step: after learning a new work skill, close the material, try to do it or explain it from memory, then check what you missed.
facts.caveat: A sensible application of the research above rather than a single tested recipe.

facts.statement: A practical step: repeat that short recall attempt on later days, with gaps between attempts, rather than all at once.
facts.caveat: Exact timing is not fixed by the research; any spaced schedule beats none for lasting retention, usually.

facts.statement: Short recall attempts can be tied to work that already happens, such as using the new tool on a real task a few days after training.
facts.caveat: Suggested way to make the habit low effort; not itself a studied claim.

facts.statement: A single training session with no follow-up leaves most of the later remembering to chance.
facts.caveat: Use as a plain-language summary of F1 to F3; do not turn it into a percentage.

not_claimed: Any specific percentage of training forgotten after a set time (such figures circulate without a reliable source)
People have learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) and learn better when taught in their style
We only use ten percent of our brains
Learners remember fixed percentages of what they read, hear or do (the 'learning pyramid')
There is one ideal gap between practice sessions that works for everyone
Quotes attributed to named people about learning that were not checked

review.note: No topic was supplied. The writer chose spaced retrieval practice as a conservative default. Reference hints are from memory and were not verified against sources; a human should confirm the topic and check the hints before approval. Suggested running situation (not a fact): a colleague trained on new software who struggles a week later.
